items.label: Figure 1
items.caption:
Fig. 1.
Feature intra-category similarity (IntraSim) and prediction visualiza-
tion. The brighter color indicates a higher IntraSim for the bus (left two columns)
and truck (right two columns). The standard feature fusion demonstrates low
IntraSim within objects and at their boundaries. We observe rapid changes
or variations in feature values within objects, i.e., disturbed high-frequency
features leading to relatively low intra-category similarity [11] and resulting in
intra-category inconsistency. Furthermore, the blurred boundary lacks accurate
high frequency, leading to boundary displacement. The proposed FreqFusion
shows more consistent features and clear boundaries, contributing to more
consistent prediction with ﬁner boundaries.

items.label: Figure 2
items.caption:
Fig. 2.
Illustration of intra-category similarity, inter-category similarity, and
similarity margin. Different colors indicate different categories.

items.label: Figure 3
items.caption:
Fig. 3.
The illustration of FreqFusion. Pixel unshufﬂe involves resizing the spatial dimensions of the feature by half and expanding the channel by a factor of 4×,
dividing them into 4 groups, such as from C × 2H × 2W to 4 × C × H × W. Pixel shufﬂe [62] is the reverse operation, transitioning from 4 × C × H × W
to C × 2H × 2W. The Adaptive Low-Pass Filter (ALPF) generator and Adaptive High-Pass in the initial fusion share the same parameters as those in the ﬁnal
fusion.

items.label: Figure 4
items.caption:
Fig. 4.
The illustration of generators in FreqFusion. ⊗represents element-wise multiplication, and ⊖represents subtraction.

items.label: Figure 5
items.caption:
Fig. 5.
Frequency analysis of the learned convolutional kernel in the ALHPF
generator is presented. In (a), the nine learned kernels for generating 3 × 3
spatial-variant low-pass ﬁlters are displayed. A brighter color indicates a higher
learned weight. (b) illustrates their corresponding Fourier-transformed kernels.
To further analyze their characteristics, we average their frequency amplitudes
and present the frequency spectrum in (c), demonstrating higher power for high-
frequency components, indicating reliance on high-frequency components in the
feature for ﬁlter prediction.

items.label: Figure 6
items.caption:
Fig. 6.
Visualization for initial fusion. In comparison with (a), the FreqFusion
recovers more detailed features in (b). Moreover, with enhanced initial fusion,
(c) exhibits clearer boundaries. (e) and (f) depict the standard variance of
predicted low-pass ﬁlters (LPF), (f) demonstrates a more effective maintenance
of boundaries.

items.label: Figure 7
items.caption:
Fig. 7.
Visualization for intra-category similarity of features. We illustrate
the intra-category similarity for the car category, and a brighter color indicates
a higher similarity. The bilinear upsampled results exhibit severe inconsisten-
cies in features and displacements along the boundaries. Our proposed ALPF
generator addresses these inconsistencies, enhancing feature consistency and
reﬁning boundaries. Furthermore, the offset generator not only further improves
feature consistency but also contributes to achieving more accurate boundary
delineations.

items.label: Figure 8
items.caption:
Fig. 8.
Illustration of how local similarity guides the offset prediction for
resampling. The brighter color indicates a higher intra-category similarity. The
3 × 3 gray grid indicates the cosine similarity Si,j between the pixel at (i, j)
and its 8 local neighbors, including itself, for better visualization. A brighter
color indicates a higher similarity. Local similarity guides the offset generator
to sample towards features with high intra-category similarity, thereby reducing
the ambiguity in boundary or intra-category inconsistent areas.

items.label: Figure 9
items.caption:
Fig. 9.
Visualization for resampling offsets predicted by the offset generator.
The offsets at the inside boundaries of the buses and cars are toward the interior
places where the features are more consistent and clear, while the offsets at the
inside boundaries are towards the contrary direction, which makes the boundary
clearer.

items.label: Figure 11
items.caption:
Fig. 11.
Quantitative frequency analysis. We present the results on a logarith-
mic scale for better visualization. It indicates that the AHPF generator enhances
high-frequency power, thereby improving the level of detail in the features and
producing clearer boundaries.

items.label: Figure 10
items.caption:
Fig. 10.
Visualization of low-level features. The AHPF generator signiﬁcantly
enhances boundaries by dynamically extracting high-frequency information
from the low level, resulting in clearer object boundaries. The red box indicates
the zoom-in area.

items.label: Figure 12
items.caption:
Fig. 12.
Visualization for feature fusion. In comparison with standard feature
fusion, the fused features obtained by FreqFusion exhibit more consistent
features with sharper boundaries. The red boxes indicate the zoom-in areas.

items.label: Figure 13
items.caption:
Fig. 13.
Visualization on the Cityscapes [96] validation set. Compared with the vanilla model SegNeXt [31] (row one), the proposed FreqFusion (row two)
considerably improves the segmentation accuracy and consistency.

items.label: Figure 14
items.caption:
Fig. 14.
Visualization on the ADE20K [33] validation set. Compared with the vanilla model SegFormer [30] (row one), the proposed FreqFusion (row two)
considerably improves the segmentation accuracy and consistency.

items.label: Figure 15
items.caption:
Fig. 15.
Visualization on the COCO [34] validation set. We select the top two best-performing methods, CARAFE [94] (row one) and Dysample [71] (row two),
excluding our proposed FreqFusion. In comparison, our FreqFusion (row three) demonstrates superior prediction accuracy and consistency.
